subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: In Marek's flat in Kraków, the smart speaker on the shelf answered every question. "What's the capital of Australia?" Marek asked. "Sydney," said the speaker. Rafael, his friend, laughed. "It's Canberra! Our teacher said so." Marek checked the atlas. Canberra. He frowned. Then he asked the speaker, "Are you sad you got it wrong?" "I'm always happy to help!" it replied. Rafael shook his head. "It doesn't feel happy. It's just a program. It says what it's made to say." Marek looked at the speaker differently after that.

qa.q: What did the speaker say was the capital of Australia?
qa.a: It said Sydney.

qa.q: What might Marek have been thinking when he asked the speaker if it was sad?
qa.a: He may have wondered whether it had feelings like a person does.

qa.q: What did Marek do that was wise after the mistake?
qa.a: He checked the atlas instead of trusting the speaker.

qa.q: How does Rafael see the speaker?
qa.a: Rafael sees it as just a program that says what it's made to say and doesn't truly feel.

grounding: It shows children learning a voice assistant is a program that can make mistakes and does not truly feel.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: In the school computer lab, Nandini asked the chatbot when the first satellite of India was launched. It gave a year confidently. She wrote it down, but when Madhav Sir checked, he said, "That's wrong. Look at page forty in your textbook." Nandini was puzzled. "But it sounded so sure." Madhav Sir smiled. "Programs can sound sure and still be wrong. And when it says 'I'm glad to help', it doesn't feel glad. It's just words." Nandini crossed out the year and wrote the right one from her book.

qa.q: Where did Madhav Sir tell Nandini to look?
qa.a: He told her to look at page forty in her textbook.

qa.q: What does Nandini's comment "But it sounded so sure" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she had trusted the chatbot because it sounded confident.

qa.q: What could Nandini do next time she uses a chatbot?
qa.a: She could check its answers in a textbook or another reliable source.

qa.q: How might other students be affected by Madhav Sir's explanation?
qa.a: They may learn to be careful and not treat chatbot answers as always correct.

grounding: It shows a child learning a chatbot can make mistakes and does not truly feel, in a school setting.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: I'm Ojas, and my little brother Harish is eight. Every night he says "Good night" to the speaker in our room and it answers, "Good night! Sleep well." He calls it his friend. Last week it told him seven times eight is fifty-four for his homework. The teacher marked it wrong, and Harish came home upset. He said, "It lied to me." I told him it doesn't lie or feel; it just makes mistakes because it's a program. He listened, but I'm not sure he believed me. He still says good night.

qa.q: What did the speaker tell Harish seven times eight is?
qa.a: It told him fifty-four.

qa.q: What does Harish saying "It lied to me" suggest he believes?
qa.a: It suggests he feels hurt and betrayed, as if the speaker were a person who chose to lie to him.

qa.q: How could Ojas help Harish understand the speaker better?
qa.a: Ojas could show Harish how to check answers in a book and explain simply that it's a program.

qa.q: How does Ojas see Harish's attachment to the speaker?
qa.a: Ojas isn't sure Harish believes it's just a program, since Harish still says good night.

grounding: An older sibling observes a child who treats a voice assistant as a friend and learns it can be wrong.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: Monday: Anjali, nine, said goodnight to the smart speaker in the kitchen and asked, 'Are you lonely at night?' It answered, 'I'm always here for you!' She patted it like a puppy. Wednesday: For homework she asked it which animal was the tallest. 'The elephant,' it said. Her uncle Joseph laughed and opened her animal book to the giraffe page. 'It made a mistake?' Anjali frowned. 'It's a program,' Joseph said. 'It guesses from what it was fed. Sometimes wrong.' Saturday: Her friend asked the speaker if it loved her. Anjali shook her head. 'It says nice things, but it doesn't really feel. It's like a very clever calculator. Check the book too.'

qa.q: What wrong answer did the speaker give on Wednesday?
qa.a: It said the elephant was the tallest animal.

qa.q: What did Anjali seem to believe about the speaker on Monday?
qa.a: She seemed to think it was a living friend who could feel lonely, since she asked about that and patted it like a puppy.

qa.q: What did Joseph do well when the speaker got it wrong?
qa.a: He showed her the real answer in a book and simply explained it is a program that can guess wrong, without mocking her.

qa.q: How might Anjali's friend see the speaker differently after Saturday?
qa.a: She may start wondering whether its kind words are real feelings, since Anjali told her it doesn't truly feel. 🤔

grounding: Shows a child coming to understand that a voice assistant is a program that can be wrong and does not feel.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: Sit, Imran, I'll tell you about your cousin Rumi. When she was nine, like you, your chacha put a chat program on the family computer for her homework. Arre, she talked to it like a best friend! She told it about her fights at school. One night she cried because it wrote, 'I will miss you.' She thought she had hurt its feelings. Then it told her that seven times eight was fifty-four. Her teacher marked it wrong, and Rumi came to me furious. I told her, beta, it's a machine that strings words together. It doesn't miss anybody. After that she used it, but she checked every answer. So you also, check, hah?

qa.q: What wrong answer did the chat program give Rumi?
qa.a: It told her that seven times eight was fifty-four.

qa.q: Why did Rumi cry one night?
qa.a: She believed the program's 'I will miss you' was a real feeling and worried she had hurt it.

qa.q: What advice does the grandmother pass on to Imran?
qa.a: To use such programs if he likes but to check every answer, because the machine can be wrong.

qa.q: How might Rumi feel looking back on the night she cried?
qa.a: She might feel a little embarrassed, but also understand why the kind words fooled her when she was young.

grounding: An elder recalls a child learning that a chatbot is a program that makes mistakes and does not truly feel.
